qt: to the Commission Leila Chaibi (The Left) Subject:

In countries such as Belgium or Denmark1, mobile EU citizens are required to register an address to obtain their right to residence in the country. This excludes people without a stable housing situation and those living in informal arrangements from obtaining residence, and therefore from accessing essential services and rights, such as social protection2, voting rights3, or opening a bank account4. However, under Directive 2004/38/EC5, having an address is not a condition for EU citizens to be able to register as a resident in another Member State. This was already made clear by the Commission in an answer to a parliamentary question in 20176. Given that this requirement is current practice in several Member States: 1.

Will the Commission investigate whether the requirement to have an address is in compliance with EU law, since it is a de facto obstacle to the exercise of the right to residence under Directive 2004/38/EC?
Will the Commission communicate with Member States on this issue, and where they require such a condition (proof of address), ask them to cease doing so?

at: (English version) to the Commission Leila Chaibi (The Left) (13 March 2024) Subject: Discrimination based on the requirement to provide proof of address to obtain residence In countries such as Belgium or Denmark (1), mobile EU citizens are required to register an address to obtain their right to residence in the country. This excludes people without a stable housing situation and those living in informal arrangements from obtaining residence, and therefore from accessing essential services and rights, such as social protectio n (2), voting rights (3), or opening a bank account (4). However, under Directive 2004/38/EC (5), having an address is not a condition for EU citizens to be able to register as a resident in another Member State. This was already made clear by the Commission in an answer to a parliamentary question in 2017 (6). Given that this requirement is current practice in several Member States: 1.

Will the Commission investigate whether the requirement to have an address is in compliance with EU law, since it is a de facto obstacle to the exercise of the right to residence under Directive 2004/38/EC?
Will the Commission communicate with Member States on this issue, and where they require such a condition (proof of address), ask them to cease doing so?

(23 April 2024) Proof of address is not a precondition for EU citizens to have a right to reside in the host Member State under EU law. Therefore, the lack of address is not a ground for refusing the issuance of a registration certificate under the Free Movement Directive 2004/38/EC. However, residence registration under that directive must be distinguished from registration in national/local population registers, which is a matter of national law. The Commission understands that all residents in Denmark, Danish and non-Danish, are required to have an address for inscription in the population register ‘CPR’. Registration in the CPR is not a condition for legal residence under EU law. Similarly, under Belgian national law, all persons residing in Belgium (whether Belgian citizens, EU citizens or third-country nationals) must register in the national population registries. In addition, persons who cannot have an official address can have a ‘reference’ address either at the address of another person or at a public social centre (CPAS). Registration in CPAS is, in particular, provided for homeless people. Registration in the national population register must not constitute an impediment to the exercise of an EU citizen’s free movement rights. The Commission will continue to monitor the implementation of EU free movement law by all Member States, including in relation to this aspect.
